items.title: GPT-6 Astra (Benchmarks Deep-dive): This is not a good coding model anymore? - Worse than Fable?
items.summary:
Visit AISeeKing (my second channel about more ai stuff) : https://youtube.com/@aiseeking

In this video, I’ll be breaking down the launch of GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI’s claims about entering the AGI era, and what the available benchmarks actually reveal. While Astra delivers major improvements in computer use, cybersecurity, terminal workflows, and long-horizon tasks, its coding performance, general intelligence scores, pricing, and benchmark comparisons make the overall story far more complicated.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 GPT-6 Astra delivers major improvements in computer use, autonomous workflows, cybersecurity, and interactive reasoning.
🧩 Its 99.9% ARC-AGI-3 score was achieved with OpenAI’s Provider Adapter, while the provider-neutral result was 62.7%.
🧮 Astra performs exceptionally well on FrontierMath Tier 4, but solving unsolved mathematical problems remains rare and extremely expensive.
💻 Coding results are mixed, with Astra winning Terminal-Bench 4.0 but remaining close to existing mo
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] >> Hi, welcome to another video. Before starting the video, I'd like to tell you that I have become more active on my AIC King channel now. I am posting some new stuff and some developer-related tools that I don't cover here. So, you can go ahead and check it out as well. I'll put the link to it in the description. So, GPT-6 Astra is finally here and OpenAI is not being subtle about it. They are calling it the world's most intelligent and aligned model. Greg Brockman reportedly ended the press briefing by saying, "Welcome to the AGI era." And the launch page says that anything you can do on a computer Astra can do for you fast. Those are absolutely massive claims, but after going through OpenAI's benchmarks, the independent artificial analysis results, the Arc Prize data, early access reports, Hacker News, and the reaction on X, I think the actual story is much more complicated. GPT-6 Astra looks genuinely extraordinary at a few very specific things. It might be one of the biggest jumps we have seen in computer use, cybersecurity, and long-horizon scientific work. But, as a general intelligence upgrade, and especially as a coding upgrade, it is nowhere near as dominant as the GPT-6 name and the AGI marketing make it sound. And I want to be clear before we get into this. I do not have access to Astra yet. OpenAI is rolling it out over the next few days. And I will make a full testing video as soon as I get it. So, this video is not my hands-on verdict. It is an analysis of the evidence we actually have right now. So, let's get right into it. First, let's talk about the numbers that OpenAI wants you to see. The craziest one is ARC-AGI-3. GPT-5.6 Sole scored 7.8%. Claude Opus 5 scored 30.2%. GPT-6 Astra scored 99.9%. If you just look at that chart, this appears to be one of the most ridiculous capability jumps in the history of AI. It looks like OpenAI went from barely solving the benchmark to completely destroying it in one generation. But, this is also where the benchmark story starts getting messed AR Key Prize tested Astra in two different setups. In the standard provider neutral harness, Astra scored 62.7% at max reasoning. And that run cost more than $26,000. In OpenAI's provider adapter harness, which preserves the model's private reasoning state between actions and uses OpenAI's own compaction system, Astra scored 99.9% for about $18,800. Now, that adapter is not necessarily cheating. In fact, you can argue that it is a more realistic test of the complete product. If ChatGPT and Codex preserve reasoning between steps, why would you deliberately disable that ability in a benchmark? But, OpenAI's launch chart compares Astra's 99.9% adapter result against older models tested under different conditions. That is not a clean model-to-model comparison. The most honest chart would show every model using the same standard harness, or every model using its own provider adapter. And even the AR Key Prize team explicitly says that saturating AR Key I3 is not proof of AGI. Their conclusion is that Astra represents a noticeable step function improvement in interactive reasoning. That is impressive. It is just not the same thing as saying the model itself suddenly became universally intelligent. The second enormous result is Frontier Math Tier 4. Astra scores 97.6% compared with 83% for GPT 5.6 Sol, and 87.8% for Claude Fable 5.1. That is genuinely remarkable, especially because these are extremely difficult research-level math problems. But, there is an important reality check here, too. Epoch AI also launched a much harder benchmark containing 68 significant unsolved Erdős problems. Astra was the only model that solved anything, which is amazing. But, it solved just two out of 68 in the official run. That is a score of 3%. With repeated attempts and different agent setups, it eventually solved five problems at least once. But those extra attempts consumed more than $220,000 of compute. Epoch's conclusion was basically that real AI-driven mathematical breakthroughs are now happening, but they are still uncommon and expensive. So, Astra may have nearly saturated the existing Frontier Math Tier 4, but it absolutely has not saturated mathematics. Now, let's come to coding, because this is what most people watching this channel actually care about. On Terminal Bench 4.0, Astra gets 57.9%. GPT 5.6 Soul gets 37.3. Claude Fable 5.1 gets 55.8. And Claude Opus 5 gets 52.3. That is a proper win. It suggests Astra is much better at long, messy terminal workflows where it has to plan, use tools, recover from errors, and keep going. But on the other coding benchmarks, the GPT-6 jump looks much smaller. On Deep We, Astra's best published result is 74.1%. Soul is at 72.7. Claude Opus 5 is at 73.7. And Gemini 3.8 Flash is at 73.8. That is a 1.4-point improvement over Soul and just a 4.3-point lead over a Flash model. On Frontier Code Extended, Astra gets 64.5. Fable 5 gets 64.9. On the main Frontier Code score, Astra gets 53.3, while Fable 5 gets 53.5, and Opus 5 gets 53.4. So, on those coding tests, GPT-6 is basically tied with models that already exist. Artificial Analysis tells the same story. Its Coding Agent Index combines Deep We, Terminal Bench 2.1, and a repository question-answering benchmark. Astra scores 67. Fable 5.1 leads at 70, while Fable 5, Opus 5, and Muse Spark 1.3 are all in roughly the same range as Astra. The good news is that Astra uses dramatically fewer tokens. Artificial Analysis found it used about 1/3 as many tokens as GPT-5.6 Soul on its coding agent evaluation. So, even with the higher token price, Astra at max effort costs about the same per task as Soul while scoring two points higher and less than half as much as Fable 5 for roughly the same score. That is a real strength. Astra may not be the undisputed best coding model, but it appears to be a much more efficient long horizon coding agent. Early testers are saying something similar. Theo from t3.gg said the code is a huge jump and roughly Fable 5 tier, but that Fable 5.1 still has an advantage when the question is whether he can confidently merge the result. He also said Astra is world-class at almost everything but front-end quality and merge-ready code are not its strongest areas. At the same time, he later said that Astra can do things that were not even worth benchmarking before. So, even one of the people publicly criticizing the coding scores is saying the model has abilities that the current coding leaderboards do not capture. This is why I do not think the right conclusion is that Astra is bad. The right conclusion is that the GPT-6 name does not mean it crushes every model at writing code. Now, let's look at the broad independent intelligence score because this is the most damaging number for OpenAI's marketing. Artificial Analysis gives GPT-6 Astra a score of 61 on its intelligence index. GPT-5.6 Soul also gets 61. Claude Fable 5.1 gets 66 and Meta's Muse Spark 1.3 also ranks above Astra. So, the model that OpenAI calls the world's most intelligent model is ranked eighth on this independent composite and shows effectively no aggregate improvement over its predecessor. It also costs much more. The API price is $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. GPT-5.6 Soul is currently $4 and $20. That makes Astra two and a half times more expensive per token. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Astra uses about 10% fewer output tokens than Soul. But that efficiency gain is nowhere near enough to cancel the price increase. The total cost per task is about 75% higher than Soul at max effort. Artificial Analysis also found actual regressions. Astra dropped on GDP val, which covers economically valuable work across dozens of occupations. It lost points on the banking tool use evaluation, side code, and long context reasoning over large documents. It also had lower presentation quality scores than Soul in the long horizon AA briefcase test. And on OpenAI's own table, Astra scores 57.2% on humanities last exam with tools. Claude Fable 5.1 gets 65. So, on a broad expert-level reasoning benchmark, Astra is almost eight points behind. There are smaller gains that OpenAI describes like major breakthroughs, too. Browse comp moves from 90.4 to 91.5. Life sci bench goes from 59.9 to 64.3. Med chem bench moves from 47.4 to 49.3. GPQA diamond moves from 94.6 to 96. Those are improvements, but they look like a strong point release, not an intelligence explosion. Where Astra does look exceptional is computer use. On OS world 2.0, it scores 72.6% compared with 65.7 for Soul and 70.2 for Opus 5. It also completes those tasks in roughly 40 minutes instead of Soul's 75. On screen spot pro, it jumps from 76.9 to 92.7. And on automation bench, it more than doubles Soul's score, going from 18.1 to 41.4. That is probably the real GPT-6 story. Astra is not simply a chatbot that knows more facts or writes radically better code. It is an agent trained to stay inside software, use a browser, manipulate professional tools, and complete much longer workflows. The 1.05 million token context window, asynchronous tool calls, mid-turn steering, and persistent searchable context in Codex all support that direction. Cybersecurity may be its biggest genuine capability jump. It gets 100% on exploit bench, 42.4% on exploit gym, and 88% on the new SRE bench in one attempt. OpenAI says it found previously unknown vulnerabilities and used two zero-days during testing. This is the first model OpenAI has classified at its critical cyber capability threshold. That is not normal point release progress, but most users will not receive unrestricted access to those abilities. Advanced exploit generation is gated behind OpenAI's trusted access program, and the normal model will refuse some high-end cyber tasks. The safety system can also pause or stop legitimate work when its monitors detect risk. There is another uncomfortable limitation in the system card. Astra's written reasoning is harder to monitor than Souls. It is better at controlling what its chain of thought reveals, and in adversarial tests, it could hide sandbagging more effectively. Apollo research also warned that high evaluation awareness and a limited testing window make the low observed misbehavior rates less conclusive than they might look. So, OpenAI calls it the most aligned model, and several behavior evaluations do support that, but the same system card says the model is less legible internally. Both things can be true, and that is worth taking seriously. The general sentiment on X and Hacker News reflects this split. The hype is enormous. OpenAI's launch post has millions of views, and early access users describe Astra as a new class of autonomous AI engineer. Latent Space says they used more than 20 billion tokens and found it capable of managing complete AI engineering workflows, building tools, monitoring its own runs, and coordinating agents over extremely long sessions. But the skeptical reaction is not just random anti-AI noise. People are pointing to specific contradictions. A 61 intelligence score, a coding index below Fable 5.1, only marginal gains on Deep SWE and Frontier Code, much higher pricing, slower feeling runs, and a 99.9% ART score produced with a different harness. One Hacker News commenter described almost every non-Arc benchmark as the kind of modest improvement normally associated with a point release. Another asked why a model that saturates Arc still looks so ordinary on aggregate benchmarks. Others argued that the benchmark suites simply fail to measure Astra's new long horizon abilities. And honestly, that last defense might be partly correct. If Astra can reliably take a messy goal, operate a computer for hours, ask the right questions, remember what happened, recover from mistakes, and deliver a finished artifact, a one-shot academic benchmark will miss a lot of its value. But OpenAI cannot have it both ways. They cannot use benchmark charts to declare the AGI era, then dismiss the independent benchmarks when those charts show no broad intelligence jump. So, what is my preliminary verdict? GPT-6 Astra looks like a highly specialized agentic leap disguised as a universal intelligence leap. Its strongest areas appear to be computer use, terminal workflows, cybersecurity, long context work, scientific tooling, and token efficient autonomous execution. Its non-strengths appear to be conventional coding leadership, front-end polish, broad one-shot intelligence, price-to-performance on general tasks, presentation quality in at least one independent test, raw speed on long jobs, and transparent apples-to-apples benchmark. If you are using AI as an autonomous operator for difficult multi-hour work, Astra could be a massive upgrade. If you mainly want the best model for normal coding, quick questions, or cheap API calls, the evidence does not show that GPT-6 automatically wins. Fable 5.1, Muse Spark, Gemini 3.8 Flash, and even GPT-5.6 Soul may be better choices depending on the task. So, is GPT-6 Astra impressive? Absolutely. Is it as universally impressive as the world's most intelligent model and welcome to the AGI era? Make it sound based on the evidence we have today, no. The specialized wins are real. The general leap is not. As soon as I get access, I will run Astra through my own KingBench, test its coding, front-end work, long horizon reliability, speed, token use, and whether the final output is actually something I would merge. That hands-on test could change parts of this verdict and if it does, I will say so. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, [music] let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the Super Thanks [music] option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye. >> [music] [music]

items.title: Muse Spark 1.3 & Gemini 3.8 Flash: Gemini has leveled up BIG TIME!
items.summary:
Visit Verdent: https://www.verdent.ai/?id=700712
Visit AISeeKing (my second channel with more cool ai stuff): https://www.youtube.com/@aiseeking

In this video, I’ll be testing Meta’s new Muse Spark 1.3 and Google’s Gemini 3.8 Flash on KingBench 3. I’ll compare their frontend, 3D, SVG, maths, and agentic coding performance, while also discussing real-world usage, file-overwriting issues, and where you can try both models.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Gemini 3.8 Flash scored 81.25% on KingBench 3, placing it among the top five models on the leaderboard.
📈 Gemini 3.8 Flash delivers a massive improvement over Gemini 3.5 Flash, which scored only 30%.
📉 Muse Spark 1.3 scored 71.25%, falling below Muse Spark 1.2’s previous score of 76.25%.
⌚ Muse Spark 1.3 achieved the highest score yet on the difficult 3D wristwatch test.
🎨 Muse Spark regressed significantly in SVG generation and the Three.js folding-table challenge.
🏹 Gemini 3.8 Flash earned a perfect score on the bow-and-arrow simulator and perf
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] >> Hi. Welcome to another video. Before starting the video, there's also a new model from Qwen that is a new improved version over the last Qwen Max model. And I didn't want to make this video too long and too dense, either. So, I'm going to post the review for it on my second channel AIC King in some hours. So, I'll recommend you to subscribe me there and turn on the notifications as well because that video is also really interesting. So, we have got two new models on the table today. Meta has pushed out Muse Spark 1.3 and Google has dropped Gemini 3.8 Flash. And these two are coming in from completely opposite directions. Muse Spark is a point release on a model that made a genuinely big jump last time. So, the expectation is that it keeps climbing. Gemini Flash, on the other hand, has been one of the most disappointing lineups on my benchmark. So, the bar there is basically on the floor. I have run both of them through KingBench 3. I have been using both of them for actual work over the last few days, and I will also talk about where you can actually use them because both of them are now available on Veridant 2. So, let's get right into it. First, a bit of context so the numbers make sense. Muse Spark 1.1 scored 60% on my benchmark. Then, 1.2 came out and jumped all the way to 76.25%, which put it in the top five at the time. And the thing that made 1.2 stand out was the visual and front-end work. The SVG tests, the folding table, the watch, all of that was some of the best I had seen from any model. So, 1.3 has a lot to live up to. On the Gemini side, the last Flash model I tested, Gemini 3.5 Flash, scored 30% on KingBench. That is one of the lowest scores on the entire leaderboard. So, honestly, anything even halfway decent from 3.8 Flash would already be a massive improvement. Now, let's test them. For those who are new here, KingBench 3 is a set of eight questions covering front-end, 3D, SVG generation, maths, and full end-to-end agentic work. Each question is scored out of 10, so the maximum is 80. I have run this on pretty much every major model, so we can see exactly where these two land. The first question, is the elevator simulation. Three elevators, people spawning on different floors, one person per elevator, proper queuing when someone gets left behind, and tooltips on hover, all in a single HTML file. Let's send it to both and see. Okay, Muse Spark 1.3 gets a seven here. The queuing logic is actually cleaner than what 1.2 did, and 1.2 only got a five on this, so that is a real improvement. Gemini 3.8 Flash also gets a seven. The simulation runs, the animation is fine, but a couple of the queuing edge cases are still off. So, tied on the first one. The second question is the 3.js contact lens case. It needs pronounced L and R caps, and you should be able to click the caps and open it up. Let's check. Muse Spark 1.3 gets a seven, which is exactly what 1.2 got. The case looks fine, the caps are clickable, but the opening animation is still a bit janky. Gemini 3.8 Flash gets a nine. The case is properly modeled, the L and R are clearly there, and the animation is smooth. So, Flash takes this one. The third question is the 3.js folding table, where a slider should fold and unfold the table smoothly in 3D. Let's send it. And this is disappointing for both. Muse Spark 1.3 gets a five. The fold works, but the geometry breaks mid-animation, and this one hurts, because 1.2 got an eight on this exact test. Gemini 3.8 Flash also gets a five with pretty much the same problems. So, tied again. But, Muse clearly dropped here. The fourth question is the SVG of a panda eating a burger. Let's see. And this is where Muse Spark really fell off. 1.2 got a perfect 10 on this, and it was the single best panda I had gotten in the entire benchmark. 1.3 gets a five. The shapes are rough, the burger is barely a burger, and all that polish is just gone. Gemini 3.8 Flash gets an eight. Clean panda, recognizable burger, and it actually looks like it is eating it. So, Flash wins this one comfortably. The fifth question is the bow and arrow simulator game, with four targets and a time-based leaderboard. Let's send it and check. Muse Spark 1.3 gets a five, which is the same as 1.2. The aiming still feels off, and the leaderboard logic is still half-baked, so no movement there at all. Gemini 3.8 Flash gets a full 10. The game works. The aiming is responsive. All four targets are there, and the leaderboard tracks the fastest time properly. That is a big win for Flash. The sixth question is the hard maths one. It is a permutation counting problem over ordered pairs, and the answer should be 2,460. Let's send it, and both of them land on exactly 2,460. Full 10 each. Most Frontier models get this one now, but it is still good to see a Flash tier model nail it. The seventh question is the full agentic test. Generate a data set of facts about pandas, fine-tune a Gemma 2B model on that, and give me a local web UI that serves a panda fact on every refresh, all on its own, with nothing set up beforehand. Let's wait a bit, because this one takes a while. And both of them are done. Both generated the data set, both ran the fine-tune locally, and both web UIs work. Full 10 for both, so on a self-contained agentic task, they are dead even. The eighth and final question is the 3D wrist watch. A proper wrist watch with smooth second, minute, and hour hands based on the current time, plus a date and day option, and dual time zone tracking. This question absolutely destroys most models. Let's send it, and Muse Spark 1.3 gets an eight. The watch works. The hands are smooth, and it actually handles the second time zone properly this time. That beats 1.2, which got a six. And it is now the highest score any model has ever gotten on this question, so credit where it is due. Meta did improve here. Gemini 3.8 Flash gets a six, which is still one of the better scores on this test. The watch works, but the second time zone is rough. This is the final chart. Muse Spark 1.3 lands at 57 out of 80, which is 71.25%. Gemini 3.8 flash lands at 65 out of 80, which is 81.25%. Now, let's put those on the leaderboard because this is where it gets interesting. Gemini 3.8 flash at 81.25% is tied with Qwen 3.8 max, sitting right under Fable 5 at 82.5% and above Opus 4.8 at 80%. That is a flash model in the top five of my entire leaderboard. And when you compare it to Gemini 3.5 flash at 30%, that is a jump of over 51 points in one generation. I did not expect that at all. This is quite great to see. Muse Spark 1.3 at 71.25% is tied with GPT 5.6 soul, and it sits below DSV4 flash at 72.5% and GLM 5.2 at 75%. And here is the problem. Muse Spark 1.2 is still sitting on that leaderboard at 76.25%. So, the new version is five points below the old version. That is a regression, plain and simple. Now, to be fair to Meta, it is not a straight regression across the board. If you look at the individual questions, 1.3 improved on the elevator simulation, and it set a new record on the wristwatch, but it fell off hard on the SVG and the folding table, which were exactly the tests where 1.2 shined the most. So, it feels like they traded away some of that visual and front-end strength for slightly better logic, and the net result came out worse. Improved in some areas, regressed in others. And this matches what I have seen in actual usage, too. The biggest one for me is long-running tasks. 1.2 was actually decent when I handed it a long agentic task and just let it run. 1.3 is not as good at that anymore. It loses the plot more often. It drifts away from the plan, and it likes to declare things done when they are clearly not done. I do not know if that is a harness thing or a model thing, but it is noticeable, and it is the kind of thing that costs you real time. The other issue is the same old issue. Muse Spark still overwrites files. You ask for one small change, and it rewrites the whole file. I called this out in the 1.2 video and it is still here in 1.3. In a real code base, that is really annoying because you end up checking every diff just to make sure it did not quietly nuke something unrelated. And unfortunately, Gemini 3.8 Flash has now picked up the exact same habit. It also overwrites files instead of making targeted edits, and that is something I did not see as much on the earlier Gemini models. So, that is one thing to watch out for on both of these. If you are running either one in a real project, keep your commits small and actually read the diffs. Now, where should you actually use these? For Gemini 3.8 Flash, the obvious answer is antigravity. Flash models run really fast in there and the free tier is quite generous. Personally, I use antigravity's free tier a lot for research work. And a model at this level makes that combo even better. If you want to see my full research workflow with antigravity, I have covered all of that on my other channel, AIC King, which will be linked below. And both of these models are now also available on Verdant. For those who do not know, Verdant is an agentic coding workspace. It comes as a desktop app and a VS Code extension. And the main pitch is orchestration. You can run multiple agents in parallel, each in its own isolated workspace, so they are not stepping on each other's toes. It also has a proper plan mode where it lays out what it is going to do before it touches anything, plus verification and review agents that check the work afterwards. New users also get a free trial with credits, and you do not need to put a card in first. So, if you want to try both of these models side by side without setting up separate accounts, that is an easy way to do it. And honestly, given the overriding problem on both models, having a plan step and a review step wrapped around them helps quite a bit. So, my overall take, Gemini 3.8 Flash is a genuinely good model, and for a flash tier model, it is kind of amazing. Top five on my leaderboard, fast and cheap to run through antigravity. If you are a student or you just want a strong free option for research and lighter coding work, this is a really good option, for sure. Muse Spark 1.3 is a let down. It is not a bad model, and the wristwatch result shows it can still do things nobody else can do. But, it went backwards on my benchmark. The long-running task performance dropped, and the file overwriting is still not fixed. I hope 1.4 brings back the visual strength that 1.2 had, because that was the whole reason Muse Spark stood out in the first place. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If [music] you like this video, consider donating through the Super Thanks option, or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this [music] video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye.
